                                      PROJECT NO. 58482


 LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT                       §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 SERVICE                                            §                  OF TEXAS


               TEXAS PUBLIC POWER ASSOCIATION' S RESPONSE TO
                        PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION


       The Texas Public Power Association (TPPA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the
proposal for publication (PFP) issued by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)
relating the creation of a large load demand management service. These comments are submitted
on behalf of TPPA and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of any individual TPPA member.

       Formed in 1978, TPPA is the statewide association for the 72 municipally owned utilities
(MOUs) in Texas. TPPA membership also includes several electric cooperatives and joint action
agencies, as well as the Lower Colorado River Authority. TPPA members serve urban, suburban,
and rural Texas and vary in size from large, vertically-integrated utilities to relatively small
distribution-only systems. We are proud to serve approximately 5.1 million Texans across the state.
Most of our members operate within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region,
though several are located within either the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) or Midcontinent
Independent System Operator (MISO) region. MOUs offer a long track record of stability, and we
serve an essential role in providing secure and reliable power to the wholesale electricity markets
in these regions, including ERCOT. Many of our member systems have been providing stable and
reliable electric service to communities in Texas for over 100 years, and collectively, our members
provide more than 13,000 MW of generation and maintain more than 8,500 miles of high-voltage
transmission assets or more than 15% of the transmission in ERCOT.

       On July 30,2026, the Commission issued a PFP, seeking comments by September 4,2026.
These responses are timely filed.




TPPA Comments                                                                         Page 1 of 11
                               I.       Responses to Commission Ouestions

1) Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is subject
to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS)
obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available but not ultimately instructed
to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated some percentage of the
market clearing price for the large load customer's availability to reduce demand during the
LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load customer
for their availability during the LLDMS obligation period?

        At this time, TPPA supports a standby payment equal to 25% of the LLDMS clearing price
for large load customers that were procured and available to curtail during an event but were not
dispatched. 1

        Further, TPPA recommends that the percentage paid to non-deployed LLDMS loads not
be specified in the adopted rule, but instead be established annually through a Commission order
subject to public comment. This approach would provide greater flexibility and allow stakeholders,
ERCOT, and the Commission to adjust the payment percentage as appropriate based on experience
with the LLDMS.



2) Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar year.
What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

        At this time, TPPA supports a $54 million budget for LLDMS. However, TPPA
recommends that the budget not be specified in the adopted rule, but instead be established
annually through a Commission order subject to public comment. This approach would provide

  available for deployment. Procurement should not, by itself, trigger a payment. Rather, a large load customer

 greater flexibility and allow stakeholders, ERCOT, and the Commission to adjust the budget as
appropriate based on experience with the LLDMS.



3) What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how far in
advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

4) Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so, what
limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

       TPPA answers Questions 3 and 4 together.

       TPPA believes that LLDMS should be available for ERCOT to use whenever it is
concerned about a potential reliability event. A reliability event could result from an extreme
weather event, a transmission emergency, or other grid conditions. For example, at the April 2026
ERCOT Board meeting, ERCOT presented that following Winter Storm Fern, the period of
greatest reliability concern occurred after the weather event had passed, when generation resources
had been depleted. Periods such as this should be eligible for ERCOT to deploy LLDMS.

       TPPA recommends that the rule not limit ERCOT' s ability to procure and deploy LLDMS
when ERCOT determines it is necessary to address a reliability concern. Rather, TPPA believes
the appropriate mechanism for limiting over-procurement and deployment of LLDMS is through
the established budget.



                          II.   Specific Recommendations bv Subsection

       Proposed 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.521(a) provides that "ERCOT
must ensure that each electric cooperative, MOU, and transmission and distribution utility serving
a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any necessary
equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed
during firm load shed." TPPA recognizes that this language mirrors the language in PURA §
39.170 and supports consistency between the rule and statute. However, TPPA believes the
Commission could make the applicability of the proposed rule clearer by replacing the term
"transmission-voltage customer" with "large load customer," consistent with the terminology used
throughout the proposed rule and the intent of the legislation.
TPPA Comments                                                                         Page 3 of 11
        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(b) provides terms used throughout the rule and their
definitions. Consistent with TPPA's recommendation above, TPPA recommends including the
term "reliability event" and defining it as "any event in which ERCOT anticipates the need for
additional dispatchable demand response, including extreme weather conditions and transmission
emergencies."

       Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(a)(1) and (b)(4) use the term "firm load shed." TPPA
recommends defining the term to clarify what constitutes "firm load shed" and to ensure the term
is applied consistently throughout the rule.

       Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(b)(1) defines an "extreme weather condition" as a weather
condition that creates a significant risk of an Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) event. Ideally, TPPA
recommends that"extreme weather condition" not be defined. As noted above, TPPA recommends
that the trigger for deploying LLDMS be based on ERCOT' s concern regarding a reliability event,
regardless of whether the reliability concern is caused by weather, a transmission emergency, or
an EEA event. Accordingly, there is little need to separately define "extreme weather condition."

       However, if the Commission determines that the term should be defined, TPPA
recommends instead utilizing the definition of"emergency" provided in § 25.53, which states, "a
situation in which the known, potential consequences of a hazard or threat are sufficiently
imminent and severe that an entity should take prompt action to prepare for and reduce the impact
of harm that may result from the hazard or threat." The definition also includes an emergency
declared by a local, state, or federal government or ERCOT.

       Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(c) provides the participation parameters for large load
customers to participate in the program. Specifically, proposed paragraph (c)(1)(B) provides that
a large load customer must pass a price-responsive test in compliance with ERCOT Protocols.
Further, proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(c)(2)(D) provides that a large load customer is ineligible to
participate in the LLDMS if it also participates in a demand response program in which the large
load customer curtails in response to wholesale electricity prices.

       TPPA recommends that the rule specifically state that participation is prohibited for large
load customers that "curtail in response to the wholesale prices of electricity," consistent with the
language in PURA § 39.170(b)(3). While the proposed rule requires large load customers to pass
a price-responsive test, the rule does not clearly establish what constitutes a passing or failing

TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 4 of 11
 result. Specifically stating that price-responsive behavior is prohibited would clarify the purpose
and application of the price-responsive test. Further, while proposed paragraph (c)(2)(D) includes
similar language, it limits the prohibition to price-responsive curtailment resulting from
participation in another demand response program. This limitation appears narrower than the
prohibition established in the statute, which prohibits curtailment in response to wholesale
electricity prices regardless of whether the response is provided through another demand response
program.

        Additionally, as proposed, the rule would allow large load customers to provide only a
portion of their load to the LLDMS. Without further clarification, it could be unclear whether the
prohibition on price-responsive behavior applies to the large load customer' s entire load or only
the portion of the load participating in the LLDMS. TPPA recommends that the rule clarify the
scope ofthis requirement.

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(c)(1)(A) provides that a large load customer must offer at
least 1 MW of demand reduction to participate in the LLDMS. TPPA recommends that the
minimum participation level instead be set at 75 MW of demand reduction. The LLDMS is a new
service specifically designed for large load customers, and the statutory threshold for participation
establishes 75 MW as the distinguishing characteristic ofthe customers the program is intended to
serve. Allowing a customer that meets the 75 MW eligibility threshold to participate by offering
only 1 MW of demand reduction creates a significant disconnect between the purpose of the
program and its participation requirements. If the program were adopted as proposed in this
rulemaking with a 1 MW threshold, then it would result in a program that is arbitrarily favoring
large load customers over 75 MW from other large customers, but who do not have 75 MWs, but
could still easily participate but for their arbitrary load level.

        Further, if the program is adopted as proposed with a 1 MW participation threshold, it
would provide a preferential benefit to large load customers that meet the 75 MW eligibility
threshold over other large load customers that fall below 75 MW but could otherwise provide the
same 1 MW of demand reduction. This creates an arbitrary distinction among large load customers
based solely on whether the customer's total load happens to exceed the statutory 75 MW threshold,
rather than on the amount of demand response the customer can provide. Requiring a minimum 75




TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 5 of 11
 MW demand reduction offer would better align the participation requirement with the purpose of
the LLDMS and ensure that the program provides a meaningful reliability benefit.

        The Commission should ensure that participation in LLDMS provides a meaningful
reliability benefit and is not merely a mechanism for otherwise eligible customers to participate in
a specialized service while offering a minimal amount of demand response. Requiring a minimum
75 MW demand reduction offer would ensure that the customers participating in LLDMS provide
a level of reliability value commensurate with the size of the customers for which the service was
created. TPPA therefore recommends that the rule require a large load customer to offer at least
75 MW of demand reduction to participate in LLDMS, consistent with the statutory threshold.

        Though TPPA believes that large load customers should be required to offer at least 75
MW of demand reduction to participate in the LLDMS, TPPA does not obj ect to providing
ERCOT with the discretion to deploy less than the full amount procured. For example, ERCOT
may procure 75 MW from a large load customer but determine during an event that it only needs
50 MW of demand reduction. In that circumstance, ERCOT should be permitted to deploy only
the 50 MW it needs rather than the full 75 MW. However, the large load customer should still
receive the applicable standby payment, based on the portion of the clearing price determined by
the Commission, for the remaining 25 MW that was procured but not deployed.

       Finally, TPPA recommends that the Commission annually review the minimum
participation level to ensure it remains sufficient and allow for adjustments as appropriate
following sufficient opportunity for public comment.

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(c)(2)(G) provides that a large load customer cannot participate
in the LLDMS if it participates in firming service under PURA § 39.1592 and 16 TAC § 25.65.
TPPA requests clarification regarding the scope of this prohibition. Specifically, TPPA
recommends that the Commission clarify whether the provision is intended to prohibit a large load
customer from participating in both programs entirely, or whether the prohibition is intended to
apply only to the same load or capacity being used to provide both services. Clarification is
necessary to ensure that the rule does not unnecessarily restrict a large load customer' s ability to
provide separate reliability services using distinct portions of its load.

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(d) provides, "ERCOT may procure LLDMS from a large load
customer on an as needed basis to help prevent an anticipated EEA event due to an extreme weather

TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 6 of 11
 condition or alleviate an actual EEA event due to an extreme weather condition." As noted above,
TPPA recommends that LLDMS be available for procurement during reliability events regardless
of whether the event is related to extreme weather conditions. Accordingly, TPPA recommends
revising this subsection to allow ERCOT to procure LLDMS whenever ERCOT determines that
procurement is necessary to address a reliability concern.2

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(d)(3)(B) provides the reasons why ERCOT must reject an
offer from a large load customer to provide LLDMS.

        Specifically, proposed paragraph (d)(3)(B)(iii) provides that ERCOT must reject an offer
submitted by a large load customer that failed to comply with ERCOT's instructions to deploy
during the previous LLDMS obligation period. TPPA recommends clarifying that this rejection
criterion is not limited to the immediately preceding LLDMS obligation period, but applies to any
prior obligation period in which the large load customer failed to comply with ERCOT' s
instructions to deploy.

        Further, TPPA recommends adding a rej ection criterion to address circumstances in which
accepting an offer could result in the LLDMS budget being exceeded. Because the total cost of
LLDMS procurement may not be known until after an event has occurred, ERCOT should not
accept an offer when doing so could reasonably result in expenditures exceeding the established
LLDMS budget.

        Finally, consistent with the recommendations made above, TPPA recommends that the
Commission not establish the LLDMS offer cap in the rule, but instead establish the offer cap
through an annual Commission order. While TPPA supports a $5,000/MWh offer cap at this time,
experience with the LLDMS after implementation may demonstrate that a different offer cap
would be more appropriate. Establishing the offer cap through an annual Commission order would
allow the Commission to adjust the cap as needed without requiring a rulemaking. Accordingly,
TPPA recommends that the offer cap be established through an annual Commission order subject
to public comment.

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(e)(3) provides that a large load customer must remain
deployed for (A) the duration ofthe EEA event, or (B) until the large load customer can be recalled



2 TPPA similarly recommends revising subsection (e)(2).

TPPA Comments                                                                         Page 7 of 11
 safely, as determined and communicated by ERCOT. TPPA recommends limiting the recall to
only when determined and communicated by ERCOT. As written, the provision could be
interpreted to allow a large load customer to end its curtailment when it believes the EEA event
has ended. However, as ERCOT has experienced previously, the period of greatest reliability risk
may occur after an EEA event, when generation resources that remained online throughout the
event begin to come offline. Accordingly, ERCOT should have the ability to maintain an LLDMS
deployment until ERCOT determines that the underlying reliability concern has ended and recalls
the large load customer.

         Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f) details the payment and charge processes for the LLDMS.
TPPA recommends clarifying that procurement alone should not entitle a large load customer to a
payment. Because the LLDMS will ultimately be funded by end-use customers, it is important to
ensure that end-use customers do not pay for a service that is not ultimately used. This approach
would also preserve the program's budget so that, when LLDMS is needed, ERCOT is not
constrained in its ability to deploy large loads for as long as necessary to address the reliability
event.
         Rather, payments should be based on whether ERCOT deploys LLDMS during the
applicable obligation period. IfERCOT does not deploy any LLDMS during an obligation period,
none ofthe procured large load customers should be eligible for payment. IfERCOT deploys some,
but not all, of the large load customers procured for the LLDMS, the large load customers that are
deployed should be eligible to receive 100% of the LLDMS clearing price, while the large load
customers that were procured but not deployed should be eligible to receive the standby payment,
at the percentage of the LLDMS clearing price determined by the Commission.

         Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(1)(A) provides that all payments provided must be based
on a single clearing price.3 TPPA requests clarification regarding how and when the clearing price
will be established, including whether the clearing price will be determined annually, for each
procurement, or on some other basis.

         Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(2) provides that ERCOT must include load reduction under
this section when calculating price adjustments for reliability deployments. While TPPA


3 TPPA also recommends confonning the terminology in proposed §§ 25.521(f)(1)(A), (f)(1)(D), and (h)(5) with
 respect to the term "clearing price."

TPPA Comments                                                                                     Page 8 of 11
 recognizes that this language mirrors the language used in the legislation, TPPA recommends that
the Commission identify the specific price adjustment contemplated by the provision, namely the
Reliability Deployment Price Adder. Specifically identifying the price adder would provide greater
clarity regarding how the load reduction is incorporated into ERCOT's pricing calculations
without changing the intent of the legislation.

         Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(3) provides that ERCOT must charge each load-serving
entity for LLDMS deployment costs based on the LSE' s load ratio share during the procurement
period.4 TPPA recommends conforming the terminology used throughout the rule, specifically the
terms "deployment costs"5 and "procurement period."6 Consistent terminology throughout the rule
will help ensure that the payment and cost-allocation provisions are applied consistently and avoid
confusion regarding whether these terms are intended to have distinct meanings.

         Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(g)(1) provides that ERCOT must establish criteria to reduce
a QSE's payment, claw back a QSE's payment, suspend a QSE from participation in LLDMS, or
any combination thereof, based on the QSE's failure to meet its LLDMS obligations. First, TPPA
requests clarification regarding when a payment would be subject to clawback, as opposed to
simply not being provided, if the large load customer fails to follow ERCOT' s instructions or fails
to be available for deployment. TPPA requests that the Commission clarify the intent and necessity
of this language in the preamble to the proposal for adoption to ensure that the mechanism for
compensating large loads is clear.

         TPPA also requests that the Commission clarify in the preamble how a QSE could fail to
meet its obligations under this section, as opposed to the large load customer failing to meet its
obligations. Clarifying the respective obligations ofthe QSE and large load customer is necessary
to ensure that any payment reductions, clawbacks, or suspensions are appropriately applied.
Notably, an QSE could represent a large load customer participating in the LLDMS. If the large
load customer fails to deploy as instructed by ERCOT, despite the QSE having provided the large




4 TPPA notes that the acronym "LSE" is used in the proposed rule without being identified. TPPA recommends
  clarifying what "LSE" is intended to mean.
5 Similar terminology is used in proposed § 25.521(f)(4) and as proposed by TPPA's under subsection (h).
6 This term appears to have a similar meaning to "obligation period," which is defined in the proposed rule. If the
  terms are intended to refer to different periods, TPPA requests clarification regarding the distinction between them.

TPPA Comments                                                                                           Page 9 of 11
 load customer with the required 24-hour notice, the QSE should not be subject to suspension for
the large load customer's failure to deploy.

       Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(h) provides after-action reporting requirements. TPPA
recommends that the report be required to be filed publicly. If the Commission determines that it
would be inappropriate for the entire report to be filed publicly, TPPA recommends that the rule
clarify which portions of the report may be filed confidentially. Further, TPPA recommends
requiring the report to include the total amount of the LLDMS budget expended and the dollar
impact of any adjustments made to the Reliability Deployment Price Adder.



                                        III.    Conclusion

       At this time, TPPA has no additional comments on the proposal for publication.

       TPPA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. As always, TPPA looks
forward to working with the Commission, Commission Staff, and stakeholders on this important
discussion in the coming months.

                 Texas Public Power Association's (TPPA) Executive Summary
•   TPPA recommends that standby payments occur only when ERCOT deploys LLDMS. Deployed
    loads receive the full clearing price, while non-deployed procured loads receive a standby payment. If
    no LLDMS is deployed, no payments should be made.
•   TPPA recommends that the standby payment percentage, budget, and offer cap not be fixed values.
    Instead, the Commission should establish it annually through an order subject to public comment.
•   TPPA recommends allowing ERCOT to procure and deploy LLDMS whenever it determines it is
    necessary to address a reliability concern, including transmission emergencies, or other grid
    conditions. The budget will serve as the appropriate limit on over-procurement and deployment.
•   TPPA recommends replacing "transmission-voltage customer" with "large load customer" to clarify
    the rule's applicability and align with the terminology and intent ofthe legislation.
•   TPPA recommends the rule clarify what constitutes a passing price-responsive test.
•   TPPA recommends clarifying that large load customers may not participate ifthey curtail in response
    to wholesale electricity prices, regardless of whether the curtailment occurs through another demand
    response program. Further, TPPA recommends clarifying whether the prohibition on price-responsive
    curtailment applies to the customer' s entire load or only the portion participating in LLDMS.
•   TPPA recommends increasing the minimum demand reduction offer from 1 MW to 75 MW
    consistent with the statutory eligibility threshold.
•   TPPA recommends clarifying whether the prohibition on participating in both LLDMS applies to the
    entire capacity of a large load or only the portion ofthe load participating in the firming service.
•   TPPA recommends clarifying that ERCOT must reject an offer from a large load customer that
    previously failed to comply with any LLDMS deployment instructions.
•   TPPA recommends allowing ERCOT to reject offers when accepting them could reasonably cause
    LLDMS expenditures to exceed the established budget.
•   TPPA recommends that an LLDMS deployment remain in effect until ERCOT determines and
    communicates that the load can be safely recalled.
•   TPPA requests clarification regarding how and when the clearing price will be established, including
    whether the clearing price will be determined annually, for each procurement, or on some other basis.
•   TPPA recommends specifying that the price adjustment referenced in the rule is the Reliability
    Deployment Price Adder.
•   TPPA recommends using consistent terminology throughout the rule, including clarifying the
    meaning of "deployment costs," "procurement period," "obligation period," "offer cap," and defining
    "reliability event" and "firm load shed."
•   TPPA requests clarification on when a QSE's payment would be clawed back versus withheld if a
    large load customer fails to comply with ERCOT's deployment instructions or is unavailable,
    including an explanation ofthe purpose and necessity ofthe clawback mechanism.
•   TPPA recommends clarifying the respective obligations of QSEs and large load customers and
    ensuring penalties are applied appropriately. A QSE should not be penalized when a large load
    customer fails to deploy despite the QSE providing the required 24-hour notice.
•   TPPA recommends that LLDMS after-action reports be filed publicly, or that the rule specify which
    portions may be confidential, and that reports include the total LLDMS budget expended and the dollar
    impact of any Reliability Deployment Price Adder adjustments.
